name: programming
subject: Programming: Python names, mutability and defaults (hand-written fixture)

propositions.name: Assignment binds names to objects
propositions.statement: In Python, assignment binds a name to an object and never copies it. After `b = a`, both names refer to the same object, so a change made in place through one name is visible through the other.

propositions.name: Mutable versus immutable types
propositions.statement: Lists, dicts and sets are mutable: they can change in place. Ints, floats, strings and tuples are immutable: operations that seem to change them build a new object instead.

propositions.name: Augmented assignment depends on mutability
propositions.statement: `x += 1` on an int builds a new int and rebinds `x`, leaving other names unchanged. `xs += [4]` on a list extends that list in place (via `__iadd__`), so every name bound to the list sees the change.

propositions.name: Default values are evaluated once
propositions.statement: A function's default argument values are evaluated once, when the `def` statement runs, and the same objects are reused on every call that omits those arguments.

propositions.name: Mutable default argument pitfall
propositions.statement: With `def add(x, items=[])` that appends `x` to `items`, calls that omit `items` all share and grow one list: `add(1)` returns `[1]`, then `add(2)` returns `[1, 2]`.

propositions.name: None sentinel for fresh defaults
propositions.statement: To get a fresh mutable default on each call, default to `None` and create the object in the body: `if items is None: items = []`. Use `is None` rather than a truthiness test, so a caller's empty list is still used.

propositions.name: Closures bind late
propositions.statement: A closure looks up its free variables when it is called, not when it is defined. So `fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]` gives functions that all return 2, the value `i` has when they run.

propositions.name: Capture a loop value with a default argument
propositions.statement: Writing `lambda i=i: i` fixes the late-binding problem: the default is evaluated when each lambda is defined, so each function keeps the value `i` had at that moment.

arguments.message:
## Names are labels, not boxes

Your surprise came from treating `b = a` as a copy. In Python, assignment never copies. It sticks a second label on the same object:

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)  # [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

Whether this bites depends on **mutability**. Lists, dicts and sets can change in place. Ints, strings and tuples can't; anything that looks like a change makes a new object.

That's why `+=` behaves differently by type. With `n = 5; m = n; n += 1`, `m` is still 5: a new int was made and `n` was rebound to it. With `xs = [1]; ys = xs; xs += [2]`, `ys` is `[1, 2]`, because a list's `+=` extends the list in place.

## Why the list kept growing

Here's your function:

```python
def add(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items
```

`add(1)` gave `[1]`, and `add(2)` gave `[1, 2]`. The default `[]` is evaluated **once**, when Python runs the `def` line, not on each call. Every call that leaves out `items` gets that same list, and `append` changes it in place.

The standard fix uses `None` as a sentinel:

```python
def add(x, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(x)
    return items
```

Use `is None`, not `if not items`. Otherwise a caller who passes their own empty list gets it silently replaced.

## Same rule, other direction

You expected `[f() for f in fs]` to give `[0, 1, 2]` and got `[2, 2, 2]`. The lambdas don't store `i`; they store a reference to the variable, and look it up when called. By then the loop has finished and `i` is 2. This is **late binding**.

The once-only evaluation of defaults, which caused the list bug, is the cure here:

```python
fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
```

Each lambda's default is evaluated when that lambda is created, so each one keeps the value of `i` at that moment.
